variants.title: 'Let your women keep silence': where does it belong?
variants.plain: No manuscript leaves out these two verses, but some place them after verse 40. Does this suggest they were a margin note added to the text?
variants.evidenceFor: That they are original: every surviving manuscript contains them, and most scholars (for example D. A. Carson, Anthony Thiselton, and many complementarian and egalitarian scholars alike) accept them as Paul's, explaining the Western placement as a scribe's rearrangement for smoother flow. Interpreters then debate what kind of speech is restricted (disruptive questions, judging prophecies, or speaking in general).
variants.evidenceAgainst: That they were a later insertion: Gordon Fee and Philip Payne argue that the floating position (in Bezae, other Western manuscripts and Ambrosiaster after 14:40) is the typical sign of a margin gloss; that the verses seem to clash with 1 Cor 11:5, where women pray and prophesy; and that marks in Vaticanus (distigmai) and a note in Codex Fuldensis may flag a known problem. Critics reply that the Vaticanus marks' meaning and date are disputed and that the clash can be explained.
variants.modern: All major translations print the verses in the usual place; some (NRSV, NET) mention the placement issue in notes. Many interpret the passage in context rather than as a later addition.
variants.significance: It bears directly on the debate about women's roles in church. A textual question here should not be used to settle the theological question, and both sides of that debate include scholars who accept the verses as original.

variants.title: 'The Son of God' in Mark's opening line
variants.plain: Does Mark open with 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God', or just 'of Jesus Christ'?
variants.evidenceFor: 'Son of God' is in Vaticanus, Bezae, Washingtonianus, a corrector of Sinaiticus and most manuscripts. It fits Mark's structure, where Jesus is called God's Son at the baptism (1:11), transfiguration (9:7) and by the centurion at the cross (15:39). Accidental omission is easy, because the titles were abbreviated (nomina sacra) and a string of similar endings could be skipped.
variants.evidenceAgainst: Absent from the first hand of Sinaiticus, Koridethi (Theta), a few other manuscripts, and Origen. Scribes were more likely to add a title of honour than drop one, and Ehrman argues it was added to stress Jesus' divinity.
variants.modern: Most translations include it, some with a note; NA28 prints it in single brackets (doubtful); the SBL Greek New Testament omits it.
variants.significance: Whatever is decided here, Mark clearly calls Jesus God's Son elsewhere, so the theology is unaffected; the question is about how Mark framed his opening.

variants.title: 'To the saints who are in Ephesus'
variants.plain: Was the letter we call Ephesians originally addressed to Ephesus?
variants.evidenceFor: 'In Ephesus' appears in Alexandrinus, Bezae, correctors of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and the vast majority of manuscripts and versions. All ancient titles say 'to the Ephesians'.
variants.evidenceAgainst: Absent from P46, the first hands of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, minuscule 1739 and Origen, who comments on the oddity of the wording without a place. Marcion called the letter 'to the Laodiceans' (Tertullian, *Against Marcion* 5.11 and 5.17). The letter is also strangely impersonal for a church where Paul spent about three years. Many think it was a circular letter to several churches, with a blank for the name or no name at all.
variants.modern: Most translations print 'in Ephesus' with a note that some early manuscripts lack it; NA28 brackets it.
variants.significance: Helps explain the letter's general tone and has been linked to the 'letter from Laodicea' in Col 4:16, though that link is speculative.

variants.title: 'Sons of Israel' or 'sons of God'?
variants.plain: When the Most High divided the nations, did he set their boundaries by the number of the 'sons of Israel' (Masoretic text) or the 'sons of God' (Dead Sea Scroll and Greek evidence)?
variants.evidenceFor: For 'sons of God': a Dead Sea Scroll (4QDeut-j) reads 'sons of God' (*bene elohim*), and the Septuagint reads 'angels of God' or 'sons of God'. The idea of nations allotted to heavenly beings while Israel is the LORD's own portion (verse 9) fits other passages about heavenly beings over nations (Dan 10:13, Dan 10:20, Ps 82). Scribes may have changed it to avoid any hint of other divine beings.
variants.evidenceAgainst: For 'sons of Israel': it is the reading of the Masoretic text and the Samaritan Pentateuch, and some argue it links the 70 nations of Genesis 10 with the 70 descendants of Jacob who went to Egypt (Gen 46:27). Defenders say the 'sons of God' reading could be an interpretive change in the other direction.
variants.modern: The ESV ('sons of God'), NRSV ('the gods'), NLT ('heavenly court') and NET ('heavenly assembly') follow the scroll; the KJV, NKJV, NIV and NASB keep 'sons of Israel', often with a note.
variants.significance: A clear case where the Dead Sea Scrolls changed modern translations, and it feeds into discussions of the 'divine council' in Old Testament theology (for example the work of Michael Heiser). Some fear it suggests polytheism; most who adopt it read the 'sons of God' as created heavenly beings under the one God.

variants.title: The missing paragraph about Nahash
variants.plain: A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel has a paragraph, not in the Masoretic text, explaining that Nahash king of the Ammonites had been gouging out the right eyes of Gadites and Reubenites before he besieged Jabesh-gilead.
variants.evidenceFor: That it is original: 4QSama contains it, and the 1st-century historian Josephus seems to know it (*Antiquities* 6.68-71). It explains the abrupt start of 1 Sam 11 and the strange demand of 11:2. The Masoretic text of Samuel is known to have suffered many copying losses; a scribe's eye could skip a paragraph between similar phrases.
variants.evidenceAgainst: That it is a later addition: it is absent from the Masoretic text and the Septuagint, and some scholars see it as an expansion explaining a puzzling story, of the kind found elsewhere in Second Temple texts.
variants.modern: The NRSV (1989) and NRSVue print it in the text; most other major translations (KJV, NIV, ESV, NASB) do not, though some mention it in a note.
variants.significance: A vivid example of the Dead Sea Scrolls possibly restoring lost text. It also shows translators disagree over how far to follow a single ancient manuscript.

variants.title: 'They pierced my hands and my feet' or 'like a lion'?
variants.plain: In Psalm 22 (verse 17 in Hebrew numbering), does the sufferer say his enemies 'pierced' his hands and feet, or 'like a lion' they are at his hands and feet?
variants.evidenceFor: For 'pierced' (or 'dug', 'bored'): the Septuagint (before Christ) reads 'they dug', as do the Syriac and some Hebrew manuscripts; a Psalms scroll from Nahal Hever (5/6HevPs) appears to read a verb form *ka'aru* rather than *ka'ari*. 'Like a lion my hands and feet' lacks a verb and is awkward Hebrew. Christians link the verse to the crucifixion, though the New Testament never quotes this line directly.
variants.evidenceAgainst: For 'like a lion': it is the reading of most Masoretic manuscripts, and lions appear in the psalm (verses 13 and 21), so the image fits. The meaning of the Nahal Hever spelling is debated, and the verb 'dig' does not normally mean 'pierce'. Jewish translations (for example the NJPS) read 'like lions [they maul] my hands and feet'. Some Christian scholars also hold that the text is uncertain.
variants.modern: Most Christian translations read 'pierced' (KJV, NIV, ESV, NASB, NKJV); some mention the alternative in a note. The NRSV (1989) reads 'my hands and feet have shriveled', and Jewish versions follow 'like a lion'.
variants.significance: Highly sensitive in Jewish-Christian debate. Accusations of deliberate tampering have gone both ways; the evidence shows a genuinely difficult text with ancient witnesses on both sides, and an honest reading should present both.

translations.name: Septuagint (LXX)
translations.translators: Jewish scholars in Alexandria (legend: 72 elders); many hands over two centuries
translations.basis: Hebrew (and some Aramaic) texts, sometimes different from the later Masoretic text
translations.approach: Varies by book: very literal (e.g. Ecclesiastes) to free (e.g. Job, Proverbs)
translations.impact: The Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the early church; quoted often in the New Testament; still the official Old Testament of the Eastern Orthodox Church; parent of many early Christian translations.

translations.name: Targums
translations.translators: Jewish synagogue interpreters and scholars (Onkelos, Jonathan and others)
translations.basis: Hebrew Bible
translations.approach: From fairly literal (Onkelos on the Torah) to expansive paraphrase with explanations
translations.impact: Began as oral explanations in synagogues when Aramaic replaced Hebrew as the daily language; written forms date from the late Second Temple period (fragments at Qumran) to the early medieval era. They show how Jews interpreted passages, including messianic readings.

translations.name: Peshitta
translations.translators: Unknown; possibly Jewish or Jewish-Christian translators for the Old Testament
translations.basis: Hebrew for the Old Testament; Greek for the New (standardised in the early 5th century)
translations.approach: Generally faithful, idiomatic Syriac ('simple' version)
translations.impact: Standard Bible of Syriac Christianity from India to Mesopotamia; its New Testament lacks 2 Peter, 2-3 John, Jude and Revelation.

translations.name: Old Latin (Vetus Latina)
translations.translators: Unknown, many independent translators
translations.basis: Septuagint for the Old Testament; early Greek manuscripts for the New
translations.approach: Mostly very literal, in everyday Latin; many differing versions
translations.impact: The Bible of the Latin church before Jerome, used by Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine; witnesses to early 'Western' Greek readings.

translations.name: Coptic versions (Sahidic and Bohairic)
translations.translators: Egyptian Christians, probably monks and clergy
translations.basis: Greek Old and New Testament
translations.approach: Fairly literal
translations.impact: Brought scripture to native Egyptians and early monasticism; the Sahidic version is an important witness to the Alexandrian Greek text, and Bohairic is still used in Coptic liturgy.

translations.name: Gothic Bible
translations.translators: Ulfilas (Wulfila), bishop to the Goths
translations.basis: Greek (Byzantine-type text and the Septuagint)
translations.approach: Very literal, following Greek word order
translations.impact: First Bible in a Germanic language; required a new alphabet; oldest major Germanic literature (Codex Argenteus).

translations.name: Vulgate
translations.translators: Jerome (with others for parts of the New Testament)
translations.basis: Hebrew for most Old Testament books; Greek for the New Testament; Old Latin revised
translations.approach: Balanced: faithful to meaning, sometimes literal, in good Latin
translations.impact: The Bible of the Western church for over a thousand years; declared 'authentic' at Trent; source of much theological vocabulary; parent of Wycliffe and Douay-Rheims.

translations.name: Old Church Slavonic
translations.translators: Cyril (Constantine) and Methodius and their disciples
translations.basis: Greek Gospels, lectionaries and Septuagint
translations.approach: Literal, shaped for worship
translations.impact: Created a literary language and alphabet (Glagolitic, later Cyrillic) for Slavic peoples; still the liturgical Bible of Russian and other Slavic Orthodox churches.

translations.name: Wycliffe Bible
translations.translators: John Wycliffe's followers, including Nicholas of Hereford and probably John Purvey
translations.basis: Latin Vulgate
translations.approach: Early version very literal; later version (around 1395) more idiomatic
translations.impact: First complete English Bible; copied by hand and banned without licence in 1409, yet widely read; linked to the Lollard movement.

translations.name: Tyndale's translation
translations.translators: William Tyndale
translations.basis: Erasmus' Greek; Hebrew for the Pentateuch and other books; Luther consulted
translations.approach: Direct, plain and rhythmic; close to the original but in natural speech
translations.impact: First printed English New Testament and first English translation from the originals; about four-fifths of the KJV New Testament keeps his wording on common estimates.

translations.name: Luther Bible
translations.translators: Martin Luther, with Philip Melanchthon and other Wittenberg colleagues
translations.basis: Erasmus' Greek New Testament (1522 NT) and the Hebrew Bible; Vulgate consulted
translations.approach: Dynamic and idiomatic, aimed at ordinary speech
translations.impact: Shaped modern German; spread Reformation ideas; placed the Apocrypha in a separate section; model for Tyndale and other Protestant translators.

translations.name: Coverdale Bible
translations.translators: Miles Coverdale
translations.basis: Tyndale where available; German (Luther, Zurich Bible) and Latin for the rest
translations.approach: Smooth and musical, secondary translation
translations.impact: First complete printed English Bible; his Psalms lived on in the Book of Common Prayer; led into the Great Bible (1539), the first English Bible authorised for churches.

translations.name: Great Bible
translations.translators: Miles Coverdale, under Thomas Cromwell
translations.basis: Matthew's Bible (Tyndale plus Coverdale), revised
translations.approach: Formal, for public reading
translations.impact: First English Bible authorised for use in churches under Henry VIII; chained in parish churches for anyone to read.

translations.name: Geneva Bible
translations.translators: English Protestant exiles led by William Whittingham
translations.basis: Hebrew and Greek, revising Tyndale and the Great Bible
translations.approach: Accurate and readable, with study notes
translations.impact: First English Bible with verse numbers throughout; the household Bible of Shakespeare, the Puritans and early American colonists; its notes provoked James I.

translations.name: Bishops' Bible
translations.translators: Anglican bishops under Archbishop Matthew Parker
translations.basis: Great Bible revised against Hebrew and Greek
translations.approach: Formal, with fewer and milder notes
translations.impact: Official church Bible meant to replace the Geneva; never popular; the official base text that the KJV translators were told to revise.

translations.name: Douay-Rheims Bible
translations.translators: Gregory Martin and colleagues at the English College, Douai and Rheims
translations.basis: Latin Vulgate, with Greek and Hebrew consulted
translations.approach: Very literal to the Latin, with Latin-based vocabulary
translations.impact: The English Catholic Bible for centuries (revised by Challoner, 1749-1752); influenced some KJV vocabulary.

translations.name: King James Version (Authorized Version)
translations.translators: About 47 scholars in six companies at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge
translations.basis: Hebrew Masoretic text; Greek Textus Receptus (Beza and Estienne editions); revising the Bishops' Bible
translations.approach: Formal equivalence with literary dignity; italics mark supplied words
translations.impact: The most influential English book; shaped English language and literature; still used by many churches, with some (the 'KJV-only' movement) holding it uniquely authoritative. Standard text today is the 1769 Blayney revision.

translations.name: Revised Version
translations.translators: British committees (with American cooperation)
translations.basis: Masoretic text; Greek text close to Westcott-Hort
translations.approach: Very formal; minimal changes to KJV style
translations.impact: First officially approved revision of the KJV and the first major English Bible to reflect the older Greek manuscripts.

translations.name: American Standard Version
translations.translators: American revision committee
translations.basis: As the Revised Version
translations.approach: Very formal; uses 'Jehovah'
translations.impact: Valued for precision; base for the RSV and NASB, and for the Living Bible paraphrase.

translations.name: Revised Standard Version
translations.translators: Committee under the National Council of Churches (Luther Weigle chair)
translations.basis: Masoretic text with Dead Sea Scrolls (Isaiah); critical Greek text
translations.approach: Formal, modern but dignified
translations.impact: Mainline standard for decades; controversial among conservatives (Isa 7:14 'young woman'); parent of the NRSV and ESV; had Catholic and ecumenical editions.

translations.name: New American Standard Bible
translations.translators: Lockman Foundation scholars
translations.basis: Masoretic text (BHK/BHS); Nestle-Aland Greek
translations.approach: Highly formal, word-for-word
translations.impact: A favourite for close study among conservative evangelicals; updated 1995 and 2020.

translations.name: New International Version
translations.translators: Committee on Bible Translation; over 100 evangelical scholars from several countries
translations.basis: Masoretic text with other ancient witnesses; eclectic Greek text
translations.approach: Balanced, leaning dynamic (thought-for-thought where needed)
translations.impact: Best-selling modern English Bible; revised 1984 and 2011; the 2011 gender-language changes were debated.

translations.name: New King James Version
translations.translators: About 130 scholars under Thomas Nelson
translations.basis: Textus Receptus (NT); Masoretic text; notes give Critical and Majority Text readings
translations.approach: Formal
translations.impact: Updates KJV language while keeping its textual base; popular with those who prefer the traditional text.

translations.name: New Revised Standard Version
translations.translators: Committee chaired by Bruce Metzger
translations.basis: BHS with Dead Sea Scrolls; UBS Greek
translations.approach: Formal-leaning, 'as literal as possible, as free as necessary'; inclusive language for people
translations.impact: Standard in academic and mainline settings; includes 4QSama paragraph at 1 Sam 10; updated as NRSVue (2021).

translations.name: New Living Translation
translations.translators: About 90 scholars revising Kenneth Taylor's Living Bible
translations.basis: BHS; UBS/NA Greek
translations.approach: Dynamic (thought-for-thought)

materials.name: Clay tablets and potsherds
materials.summary: Across the ancient Near East, writing was pressed into clay tablets (Babylon, Assyria) or written in ink on broken pottery called ostraca. Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on a clay brick, and Jeremiah's purchase deeds are stored in a clay jar to last. In Israel, letters written on potsherds (such as those from Lachish, around 588 BC) show soldiers' messages during the Babylonian invasion.

materials.name: Stone and plastered stone
materials.summary: Stone was for permanent, public writing. The Ten Commandments were written on stone tablets, and Israel was told to write the law on large plastered stones at Mount Ebal. Job wishes his words were carved in rock with an iron tool and lead. Inscriptions like the Siloam tunnel inscription and the Mesha Stele (which mentions Israel's king Omri) are stone texts from biblical times.

materials.name: Papyrus
materials.summary: Papyrus was made in Egypt from strips of reed pith laid crosswise, pressed and dried into sheets that could be glued into rolls. It was cheap and common in the Greco-Roman world. Most early New Testament manuscripts (P52, P46, P66, P75) are papyrus. It survives mainly in dry climates like Egypt's, which is why so many early fragments come from there. When John writes he does not want to use 'paper and ink', the word means papyrus.

materials.name: Parchment and vellum
materials.summary: Parchment is animal skin (sheep, goat or calf) scraped, stretched and dried; fine calf skin is called vellum. It is far more durable than papyrus and can be scraped and reused (a palimpsest). Most Dead Sea Scrolls are on parchment, and from the 4th century the great Christian codices were too. Paul asks Timothy to bring 'the books, especially the parchments'.

materials.name: Scroll versus codex
materials.summary: A scroll is a long roll read by unrolling from one end to the other; Jewish scripture used scrolls and still does in synagogue worship. A codex is the ancestor of the modern book: sheets folded and bound at the spine. Early Christians adopted the codex unusually quickly, perhaps because it was cheaper (both sides used), easier to search, and could hold several books together (all four Gospels, or Paul's letters). Revelation's sealed scroll and Jesus' reading from an Isaiah scroll reflect the older format.

materials.name: Ink and pens
materials.summary: Ancient ink was usually carbon (soot mixed with gum and water), which is black and stable; later iron-gall ink (from oak galls and iron salts) was common in medieval manuscripts and can eat into the page. Scribes used reed pens on papyrus and later quills. Jeremiah's scroll is written in ink, and a scribe in Ezekiel's vision carries a writing case.

materials.name: Scribes and copying
materials.summary: Scribes were trained professionals in royal courts and temples (like Shaphan and Baruch), later teachers of the law (like Ezra). Paul usually dictated to a secretary (Tertius names himself in Romans) and signed in his own hand. Early Christian copies were often made by literate believers rather than professional scribes, which led to more variation at first. Scribes made predictable kinds of mistakes: skipping lines between similar endings, swapping letters, harmonising parallel passages, and occasionally changing wording on purpose to clarify or protect doctrine. Textual critics study these patterns to work back to earlier forms. Revelation's warning against adding or taking away shows awareness of the danger.

materials.name: Masoretic notes and safeguards
materials.summary: Jewish scribes developed strict rules for copying Torah scrolls (recorded in later tractates like *Soferim*): exact materials, spacing, and correction procedures. The Masoretes (around 700-1000) added vowel points and accents and margin notes counting words and letters, marking unusual forms, and noting where the written text (*ketiv*) is read aloud differently (*qere*), as with God's name YHWH read as *Adonai*. Their care explains the remarkable stability of the medieval Hebrew text, though the Dead Sea Scrolls show that before standardisation there was more variety. Jesus' saying about the smallest letter and stroke of the law reflects the care given to the written text.

materials.name: Printing and paper
materials.summary: Paper, made from rags and plant fibre, spread from China through the Islamic world to Europe by the 12th-13th centuries. Combined with Gutenberg's movable type (around 1455), it made Bibles affordable and identical copies possible, enabling vernacular Bibles, chapter-and-verse references, concordances and eventually mass distribution by Bible societies. Isaiah's picture of God's word that does not return empty is often quoted in that missionary movement.
